overview: Two categories of antimicrobial action, distinguished by whether bacteria are killed outright or simply prevented from multiplying.
genZNote: Bactericidal: game over. Bacteriostatic: pause button, immune system finishes the job.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueB: Agents that inhibit bacterial growth and reproduction without necessarily killing the organism.

aspects.label: Mechanism of Action
aspects.valueA: Often disrupt cell wall synthesis (beta-lactams) or cause irreversible damage (e.g. DNA damage by fluoroquinolones).
aspects.valueB: Often inhibit protein or nucleic acid synthesis reversibly (e.g. tetracyclines, macrolides at standard doses).

aspects.label: Dependence on Host Immune System
aspects.valueA: Effective even in immunocompromised patients since the drug itself eliminates the organism.
aspects.valueB: Relies more on a functioning host immune system to finally clear the growth-arrested bacteria.

aspects.label: Laboratory Distinction
aspects.valueA: Subculturing onto antibiotic-free media shows no regrowth (measured via MBC).
aspects.valueB: Subculturing onto antibiotic-free media shows regrowth once the agent is removed (measured via MIC without further kill).

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Inhibits growth; bacteria may resume growing once the drug is removed.

overlay.commonMisconception: The bactericidal/bacteriostatic distinction is somewhat concentration- and organism-dependent — some agents are bacteriostatic at low doses and bactericidal at higher ones.
